newsitem.title: USA: Church of Scientology says German offer a stunt.
newsitem.headline: Church of Scientology says German offer a stunt.

text.p: The Church of Scientology has condemned as a public relations stunt, a German government invitation to entertainment executives to visit Germany to investigate reports of discrimination against church members.

In a statement issued late on Monday the Los Angeles-based Church said German leaders were ignoring several reports by international human rights organisations criticising Bonn for discrimination against minorities.

Heber Jentzsch, president of the Church of Scientology International, said the offer by Johannes Gerster, leader of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats in the state of Rhineland-Palatinate to visit Germany was just a stunt.
He likened it to the "the wolf asking the shepherd to visit his den and quickly hiding the blood and bones of the murdered sheep until he is gone."
The broadside from the Church of Scientology was the second against Germany in four days.
On Saturday, it accused Kohl of arrogance for refusing to reply to accusations that Germany was oppressing Scientologists in the same way Hitler persecuted Jews.
The accusations were contained in an open letter printed as a full-page advertisement in the Paris-based International Herald Tribune last Thursday.

Signed by actors Dustin Hoffman and Goldie Hawn, director Oliver Stone, novelists Mario Puzo and Gore Vidal along with 21 other entertainment figures, the letter urged Kohl to put "an end to this shameful pattern of organised persecution" which it compared to Nazi Germany's treatment of the Jews in the 1930s."

German political leaders and editorialists angrily denounced the writers of the letter for likening contemporary Germany to Nazi Germany and Kohl said he had no plans to respond to the letter, adding it was written by people who were only displaying their ignorance of Germany.
Los Angeles-based entertainment lawyer Bert Fields, who placed the Herald Tribune ad, spoke to Reuters about Bonn's refusal to answer the open letter.
"The emptiness of their position is shown by the fact they couldn't deny any of the factual allegations. All they could do was to use perjorative terms like 'rubbish', 'a disgrace' etc.," he said.

"The second thing they did, which was demagogic, was to say we were comparing the treatment of Scientologists to Auschwitz, and of course we didn't do that. We were comparing it to what happened to the Jews in Germany in the early 30's. We are not comparing it to death camps and we weren't saying Scientologists are put in death camps," said Fields.
Scientology is an applied religious philosophy founded in 1954 by U.S. writer and philosopher Ron Hubbard.
